## Summary

Demonstrate the reasoning layer that synthesizes analysis, classification, and library data to provide actionable recommendations. Intelligence is assistive -- it suggests, the human decides.

## User Story

As a developer managing a sound library, I want an intelligent assistant that audits my library for gaps and redundancy, recommends sounds for specific use cases, and suggests exploration targets so I can build a complete, high-quality sound collection efficiently.

## What the User Sees

```bash
toneforge intelligence audit --library ./library
toneforge intelligence recommend --use-case "sci-fi menu navigation" --max-results 5
toneforge intelligence suggest-exploration --recipe footstep-stone
```

## New CLI Commands

- `toneforge intelligence audit --library <dir>`
- `toneforge intelligence recommend --use-case <desc> --max-results <n>`
- `toneforge intelligence suggest-exploration --recipe <r>`

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Audit identifies coverage gaps, redundancy, and quality issues
2. Recommendations include confidence scores and explanations
3. Exploration suggestions reference specific recipes and seed ranges
4. No Intelligence action modifies library data without human approval
5. All suggestions reference actionable CLI commands

## Reference PRDs

- `INTELLIGENCE_PRD.md`
- `docs/prd/DEMO_ROADMAP.md` (Demo 11)

## Dependencies

- Demo 7: Library (prerequisite)
- Demo 10: Mixer (prerequisite)

## Summary

Transform curated library content into platform-specific, production-ready artifacts. The Validator ensures quality standards before compilation. The Compiler decides what stays procedural vs. what gets baked to WAV, and packages everything for target platforms.

## User Story

As a developer preparing for release, I want to validate my sound library against platform-specific quality rules and compile it into optimized, production-ready packages with deterministic build manifests.

## What the User Sees

```bash
toneforge validate --library ./library --ruleset mobile --strictness warning
toneforge compile --library ./library --category weapon --target web --rules presets/compile/web_defaults.json --output ./dist/web/
toneforge compile --library ./library --target mobile --rules presets/compile/mobile_aggressive.json --output ./dist/mobile/
toneforge compile --library ./library --target web --dry-run
```

## New CLI Commands

- `toneforge validate --library <dir> --ruleset <name> --strictness <level>`
- `toneforge compile --library <dir> --category <c> --target <platform> --rules <file> --output <dir>`
- `toneforge compile --dry-run`

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Validator checks: peak clipping, duration bounds, silence ratio
2. Validator produces structured JSON report with pass/warning/error counts
3. Compiler produces WAV files + manifest.json for target platform
4. Dry-run shows decisions without writing files
5. Build hashes enable deterministic build verification

## Reference PRDs

- `COMPILER_PRD.md`, `VALIDATOR_PRD.md`
- `docs/prd/DEMO_ROADMAP.md` (Demo 12)

## Dependencies

- Demo 7: Library (prerequisite)
- Demo 11: Intelligence (prerequisite)

## Summary

Extend ToneForge beyond audio. The Visualizer generates deterministic, audio-synchronized visual effects. Haptics produces tactile feedback patterns. Palettes coordinate the aesthetic across all outputs.

## User Story

As a game developer, I want ToneForge to generate synchronized visual effects and haptic feedback patterns alongside audio so that all sensory outputs are perceptually aligned and aesthetically coordinated through palettes.

## What the User Sees

Web demo with visual canvas:
```
> palette.set("sci_fi_neon")
> runtime.play("weapon-laser-zap", { seed: 42, visual: true, haptic: true })
  [Audio: laser zap plays]
  [Visual: cyan directional streak, 150ms]
  [Haptic: sharp pulse, 50ms, intensity=0.8]
> palette.set("organic_forest")
> runtime.play("footstep-stone", { seed: 42, visual: true, haptic: true })
  [Visual: subtle ground ripple, earth tones]
  [Haptic: soft thump, 30ms, intensity=0.4]
```

```bash
toneforge visualize export --recipe weapon-laser-zap --seed 42 --format spritesheet --frames 8 --output ./vfx/
```

## New CLI Commands

- `toneforge visualize export --recipe <r> --seed <n> --format <f> --output <dir>`

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Visualizer produces animated effects synchronized to audio events
2. Haptic patterns match audio intensity and timing
3. Palette changes visually and perceptually alter all outputs
4. Sprite sheet export produces usable game assets
5. All outputs are deterministic for the same seed and palette

## Reference PRDs

- `VISUALIZE_PRD.md`, `HAPTICS_PRD.md`, `PALLETE_PRD.md`
- `docs/prd/DEMO_ROADMAP.md` (Demo 13)

## Dependencies

- Demo 9: Runtime & State (prerequisite)
- Demo 10: Mixer (prerequisite)

## Summary

Demonstrate structured human goal representation and long-term experiential recall. Intent translates high-level directives ("make combat punchier") into actionable Intelligence queries. Memory tracks how assets are used, evaluated, and evolved over time.

## Prerequisite Demos

- Demo 11: Intelligence -- Assisted Decision-Making (TF-0MLXF98WZ1LQGM5W)

## New Modules

Intent, Memory

## What the User Sees

- Submit a structured intent: `toneforge intent submit --goal "reduce repetition in footstep sounds" --scope footsteps`
- Intelligence analysis produces actionable suggestions with human approval gate
- Query memory for historical context: `toneforge memory query --scope "weapon sounds" --time-range "last 30 days"`
- Memory informs intelligence recommendations via `--use-memory` flag

## New CLI Commands

- `toneforge intent submit --goal <desc> --scope <scope>`
- `toneforge memory query --scope <desc> --time-range <range>`
- `--use-memory` flag on intelligence commands

## Key Proof Points

- High-level goals translate into concrete, executable actions
- Memory prevents repeating mistakes and surfaces patterns humans miss
- Intent -> Intelligence pipeline maintains human approval at every step
- Historical data improves recommendation quality over time

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Intent submission produces an Intelligence analysis with actionable suggestions
2. No action executes without human approval
3. Memory records generation, promotion, and rejection events
4. Memory queries return time-scoped, scope-filtered reports
5. Intelligence recommendations improve when memory data is available

## Reference PRDs

INTENT_PRD.md, MEMORY_PRD.md

## Summary

Demonstrate ToneForge operating across multiple clients in sync and embedded within external tools. Network replicates behavioral events (not audio streams) for deterministic multi-client playback. Integrations show ToneForge driving sound in a CI pipeline and exporting to game engine formats.

## Prerequisite Demos

- Demo 9: Runtime & State -- Real-Time Behavioral Sound (TF-0MLXF8TBT0DJDCO1)
- Demo 12: Compiler & Validator -- Production-Ready Assets (TF-0MLXF9FWG18T2ZHD)

## New Modules

Network, Integrations

## What the User Sees

**Network (two browser windows side by side):**
- Host broadcasts state changes to connected peers
- Client receives state changes and plays deterministically identical audio
- State transitions are synchronized across all connected clients

**Integrations (CI pipeline):**
- Generate, validate, compile, and export sounds in automated pipelines
- Export for Unity/web with platform-appropriate file structure

## New CLI Commands

- `toneforge sync --target <engine> --library <path> --output <path>`
- Network API: `network.host()`, `network.join()`

## Key Proof Points

- Network sync uses behavioral events (~50 bytes each), not audio streams (~1 MB/s)
- Determinism guarantees identical playback on all clients from the same events
- CI integration enables automated sound generation, validation, and packaging
- Engine adapters map ToneForge categories to platform-specific audio groups

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Two clients play the same sound sequence from shared behavioral events
2. Network bandwidth is under 1 KB/s for typical gameplay
3. CI pipeline validates, compiles, and exports without manual intervention
4. Unity/web export produces platform-appropriate file structure
5. Late-join clients receive state snapshot and sync correctly

## Reference PRDs

NETWORK_PRD.md, INTEGRATIONS_PRD.md

## Summary

Demonstrate publishing and consuming ToneForge assets through a marketplace. Assets are procedural systems (recipes, stacks, sequences, palettes), not static audio files -- buyers get infinite variation from a single purchase.

## Prerequisite Demos

- Demo 12: Compiler & Validator -- Production-Ready Assets (TF-0MLXF9FWG18T2ZHD)
- Demo 15: Network & Integrations -- Distributed & Embedded (TF-0MLXFBHHW1BBO1ZJ)

## New Modules

Marketplace

## What the User Sees

- Browse marketplace listings: `toneforge marketplace search --category "sci-fi weapons"`
- Install packages: `toneforge marketplace install industrial_lasers@2.1.0`
- Use installed recipes immediately with local registry
- Publish own packages with validation: `toneforge marketplace publish --package ./my-recipes/ --name "organic_footsteps" --version 1.0.0`

## New CLI Commands

- `toneforge marketplace search --category <c>`
- `toneforge marketplace install <package>@<version>`
- `toneforge marketplace publish --package <dir> --name <n> --version <v>`

## Key Proof Points

- Marketplace assets are procedural systems, not static files -- infinite variation from a single package
- Validator gates publishing -- no broken or invalid assets reach the marketplace
- Semantic versioning ensures compatibility
- Installed recipes integrate seamlessly with the local registry

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Search returns relevant packages with metadata (recipes, stacks, ratings, license)
2. Install adds recipes to the local registry and they work immediately
3. Publish validates the package before uploading
4. Installed packages maintain determinism (same seed = same output)
5. Version conflicts are detected and reported

## Reference PRDs

MARKETPLACE_PRD.md

# Realtime adjustment of parameters — Intake Brief

## Headline

Allow continuous/looping sounds (initially vehicle engines) to have their parameters
modulated during playback, via the Runtime API defined in `RUNTIME_PRD.md`.

## Problem statement

Some sounds — engine noise being the motivating example — need to vary while they play
(pitch/RPM, filter, intensity) rather than being fixed at trigger time. The Runtime
currently exposes per-event parameters only; there is no way to change a parameter of a
sound that is already playing.

## Users

- Game developers who need engine/loop sounds to respond continuously to gameplay state
  (RPM, load, speed).
- Example user stories:
  - As a game audio developer, I want an engine loop's pitch to track RPM while it
    plays, so the sound feels connected to the vehicle.
  - As a developer, I want to set a named parameter on a playing sound, so I can
    modulate it from game logic without restarting it.
  - As a maintainer, I want parameter changes to remain deterministic, so playback stays
    reproducible.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `setSfxParameter(id, name, value)` (per `RUNTIME_PRD.md` §6) updates a parameter of a
   currently playing sound in real time; the first supported scope is continuous/looping
   sounds only.
2. Engine-style pitch/RPM modulation is supported, consistent with `CORE_PRD.md` §6.5
   (loop + oscillator/LFO pitch modulation).
3. Parameter changes are deterministic: a given seed and ordered sequence of parameter
   events produce identical output.
4. Invalid parameter names or out-of-range values are rejected with actionable errors
   and do not corrupt playback state.
5. Unit tests cover successful modulation, determinism, and invalid-input handling, plus
   at least one demonstrable engine-style user story.
6. All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code
   comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
7. Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.

## Constraints

- Scope is limited to focused continuous-sound parameter modulation (producer decision,
  parent Appendix Q3). General real-time parameter automation for arbitrary sounds is a
  documented future extension (`RUNTIME_PRD.md` §16) and out of scope.
- Must not break existing Node or browser workflows.

## Existing state

- `RUNTIME_PRD.md` §4.1 lists "optional parameter overrides"; §6 defines
  `setSfxParameter(id, "intensity", 0.5)`; §16 lists "Runtime parameter automation" as
  a future extension.
- `CORE_PRD.md` §6.5 designs vehicle engines as a looping sample with LFO pitch
  modulation.
- `src/runtime/` orchestrates state/context/sequences; runtime audio playback wiring is
  being addressed separately by TF-0MM4M1NXU0WHH6AJ and TF-0MUUB39EL000YCT0.

## Desired change

- Implement `setSfxParameter` on the Runtime, scoped to continuous/looping sounds.
- Expose it through the public runtime API and cover it with tests.

## Key Files (predicted)

- `src/runtime/runtime.ts` — add `setSfxParameter`/parameter state.
- `src/runtime/index.ts` — export the new API surface.
- `src/runtime/runtime.test.ts` — modulation and determinism tests.
- `docs/prd/RUNTIME_PRD.md` — confirm/adjust the parameter API description.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Risk:** depends on runtime→audio playback wiring that is still in flight.
  *Mitigation:* implement against the Runtime API surface and keep it backend-agnostic;
  record a possible blocking relationship with TF-0MM4M1NXU0WHH6AJ.
- **Risk:** scope creep into general automation. *Mitigation:* limit to continuous
  sounds; defer general automation to a future item.
- **Assumption:** `setSfxParameter` is the agreed API name (from `RUNTIME_PRD.md` §6).

## Related work

- `docs/prd/RUNTIME_PRD.md` §4.1, §6, §16 — parameter API and future automation.
- `docs/prd/CORE_PRD.md` §6.5 — engine loop + modulation design.
- TF-0MLXF8ZW21HJLFOG / TF-0MLXF8TBT0DJDCO1 — Demo 10 / Demo 9 runtime context.
- TF-0MM4M1NXU0WHH6AJ — Revisit runtime PRD (possible prerequisite).
- TF-0MUUB39EL000YCT0 — Make Runtime browser-aware (related playback work).
## Related work (automated report)

### Related work items
- **TF-0MUUP5HYY006XQN2** – Create cross-platform AudioContext abstraction (open)
- **TF-0MM79F5ON0GSX3CS** – Discard & Removal Recipes (Tier 4) (completed)
- **TF-0MM0AJ6R01H1XLVU** – Classification Engine Core & Types (completed)

### Repository file matches
- `standups/2026_10_05.md` — matched: add, allow, already, api, arbitrary (+122 more)
- `docs/prd/DEMO_ROADMAP.md` — matched: acceptance, actionable, add, adjust, already (+117 more)
- `demos/card-game-sounds.md` — matched: add, audio, break, brief, change (+67 more)

## User Story
As a game developer, I want ToneForge to generate synchronized visual effects alongside audio so that players receive coherent visual feedback matched to the sound design.

2. Palette changes visually alter generated effects in a consistent way.

4. Visual output is deterministic for the same seed and palette.

## Goal

Stop the CLI integration test for malformed presets from writing into the shared
`presets/sequences/` directory, so a leaked or in-flight fixture can never make
unrelated tests fail and turn a full `npm test` run red.

## Context (discovered-from: TF-0MUWK92C10094X5I)

Found while investigating the auto-created test-failure item
TF-0MUWK92C10094X5I ("<suite exited 1>: npm --silent test"). That item was
concurrently closed as a false blocker and attributed to a `node-web-audio-api`
`startRendering()` flake. This is a **separate, independently reproducible**
suite-failure mechanism that is not yet tracked.

## Root cause

`src/cli.yargs.integration.test.ts` ("returns non-zero for a malformed preset
file") writes a malformed fixture directly into the shared, repo-tracked preset
directory:

    join(PROJECT_ROOT, "presets", "sequences", "__malformed_test__.json")

and removes it in a `finally` block.

Other test files discover and parse **every** `.json` in that same directory:

- `src/sequence/golden-fixtures.test.ts` (`discoverPresets()` → `readdirSync(PRESETS_DIR)`)
  registers 3 `it.each` tests per discovered file.
- `src/cli.yargs.integration.test.ts` itself has `list sequences --json` tests
  that expect exit code 0.

Consequences:

1. **In-flight race (parallel workers):** while the malformed test is running,
   any concurrently-executing test that reads `presets/sequences/` sees the
   invalid JSON and fails.
2. **Persistent poisoning (killed run):** if a run is interrupted/timed out
   (e.g. the test-skill timeout or a SIGKILL) the `finally` cleanup never runs,
   leaving `__malformed_test__.json` on disk. Every later full run then fails
   `golden-fixtures` deterministically. The file is **not** covered by
   `.gitignore`, so it is also an accidentally-committable untracked artefact.

This matches the observed signature: a leaked `presets/sequences/__malformed_test__.json`
was present in `git status` at the start of the TF-0MUWK92C10094X5I session.

## Reproduction / evidence

With the leaked fixture present:

    printf '{ this is not valid json' > presets/sequences/__malformed_test__.json
    npx vitest run src/sequence/golden-fixtures.test.ts

Result (deterministic):

    Test Files  1 failed (1)
         Tests  3 failed | 84 passed (87)
    Error: Failed to parse sequence preset '.../presets/sequences/__malformed_test__.json'

The 3 failures are exactly the `it.each` cases for `__malformed_test__.json`
(timeline, 10-run audio determinism, 10-run simulation determinism) — i.e. a
full-suite `Test Files failed` / exit code 1.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The malformed-preset integration test no longer writes any file into the
   shared repo `presets/sequences/` (or `presets/stacks/`) directory; the
   malformed fixture is created only in an isolated temporary directory that the
   CLI is pointed at.
2. A stray/leaked `presets/sequences/*.json` fixture cannot cause unrelated
   tests (`golden-fixtures.test.ts`, `list sequences` success tests) to fail.
3. Regression coverage proves the isolation — e.g. the malformed-file path is
   detected in a temp directory, and `golden-fixtures` discovery ignores
   test-fixture artefacts — asserting observable behaviour, not source text.
4. Full project test suite passes (`/skill:test`, `--type full`).
5. Any documented behaviour added (e.g. a directory override) is documented;
   when no documented behaviour changes, the completion comment records
   documentation as not applicable.

## Suggested approach

Give the `list sequences` / `list stacks` command an explicit directory source
(e.g. a `--dir <path>` option and/or a `TONEFORGE_SEQUENCES_DIR` /
`TONEFORGE_STACKS_DIR` environment override, mirroring the existing
`TONEFORGE_RECIPE_DIR` pattern in `src/core/recipe.ts`). The malformed test then
creates its fixture in a `tmpdir()` and passes that directory to the CLI,
removing the shared-directory write entirely. Add a defensive filter so
`golden-fixtures` discovery skips `__`-prefixed test artefacts.

## References

- `src/cli.yargs.integration.test.ts` — malformed-preset test (line ~331)
- `src/cli/commands/list.ts` — hardcoded `RESOURCE_DIR` + `listPresets()`
- `src/sequence/golden-fixtures.test.ts` — shared-directory discovery
- `src/core/recipe.ts` — existing `TONEFORGE_RECIPE_DIR` directory-override pattern
- Related closed item: TF-0MUWK92C10094X5I
- Related follow-up (different root cause): TF-0MUWLQ8SS0006C9J
data.title: Harden CLI tests: malformed-preset test pollutes shared presets/sequences directory
